description: I am Himanshu pursuing Btech in Computer Science Engineering specializing in AI&ML from SRM University, Kattankulathur, Chennai. I am interested in Machine Learning, Deep Learning, LLM, Data Science.
summary: On a long mission to the Moon or Mars, the crew can’t count on Earth to catch a health problem in time. Messages can take up to 20 minutes each way, and sometimes there’s no link at all. We built ARES (Autonomous Risk Evaluation & Emergency Support), an onboard health assistant that watches each astronaut’s vital signs, learns what normal looks like for that specific person, and flags changes early. When something looks wrong, it shows exactly which part of the body is affected on a 3D model, explains why the alert was raised, and walks the crew through the matching onboard procedure. Everything runs on the spacecraft’s own computer, with no internet needed.
details:
ARES keeps a digital twin for every crew member. Instead of using fixed hospital limits, it builds a personal baseline from each astronaut’s own heart rate, heart-rate variability, blood oxygen, breathing rate, blood pressure and temperature. Machine-learning models look for unusual combinations of readings and estimate the risk of things getting worse in the next 30 minutes. Each alert comes with a plain-language explanation and a confidence level, so the crew knows why ARES is concerned and how sure it is.

The 3D hologram is the heart of the interface. Affected organs light up in colour by severity, and clicking an organ opens a panel with the actual readings compared with that astronaut’s usual values. The panel also shows the evidence behind the alert, the immediate steps from the onboard protocol database, possible long-term effects, and the history. Organs we can’t monitor are shown in grey with a note saying so, instead of being shown as healthy.

The crew can also take a short reaction-time test (PVT-B) to track alertness and fatigue. Every test, check-in and lab entry is saved permanently, so the team can see trends across the whole mission. There’s an emergency workflow, mission simulation scenarios, and a desktop app that starts with a double-click and keeps working if the computer crashes or loses power.

We were careful about honesty. ARES never diagnoses or starts a medical action on its own. It supports the crew medical officer, who makes the decisions. The crew vital signs in the demo are simulated, and every screen labels what is measured, what is estimated and what comes from research.

Tools: Python, FastAPI, SQLite, scikit-learn and SHAP for the backend and ML; React, TypeScript, Three.js and Plotly for the interface; PyInstaller for the desktop app.

Use of NASA Data

We used real NASA data to ground and check our work. NASA OSDR spaceflight studies on muscle and bone changes are shown as research evidence on the matching body regions. The RadLab and Space Radiation Analysis Group (SRAG) dose data drive the radiation exposure estimates, and NASA DONKI space-weather events feed the solar particle event alerts. We also used PhysioNet heart recordings to test our heart-signal processing, and NASA’s published bone-loss figures for the skeletal estimates.
